title: Valproic Acid Enhances the Anti‐Cancer Effect of L‐Ascorbic Acid by Upregulating Sodium‐Dependent Vitamin C Transporter 2 in Colorectal Cancer
content: Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid (AA), functions as a pro-oxidant in cancer at high doses and exerts anti-cancer effects by generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and selectively damaging cancer cells. However, low-dose AA reportedly promotes cell proliferation. Accordingly, the effectiveness of high-dose AA therapy is governed by the level of sodium-dependent vitamin C transporter 2 (SVCT2), as it regulates AA uptake. In a neuronal model, valproic acid (VPA) increased SVCT2 expression and enhanced AA uptake. Therefore, we examined the potential anti-cancer effects of VPA and AA in cells with low SVCT2 expression, including HCT-116 and DLD-1 colorectal cancer cells. In both cell lines, VPA increased the SVCT2 expression. Co-treatment with AA and VPA increased the apoptotic cells, and intracellular AA uptake and ROS generation were enhanced in both cancer cell lines. Co-treatment with AA and VPA exerted a synergistic anti-cancer effect, suppressing the hormetic dose response of AA in both cell lines. In shSVCT2-silenced cells, VPA significantly increased SVCT2 expression. The co-treatment reduced intracellular AA uptake, ROS generation, apoptosis rates, and anti-cancer effects in shSVCT2 cells. In a xenograft mouse model, the co-treatment decreased the tumor size and increased the percentage of tumor growth inhibition ratio compared with treatment with AA or VPA alone. In addition, VPA and the co-treatment increased mSVCT2 expression in the tumor. Accordingly, VPA treatment could enhance SVCT2 expression in colorectal cancer cells, suppressing the hormetic dose-response effect of AA and improving the potential of high-dose AA therapy as an anti-cancer agent.
